content: Peripheral neuropathies encompass a diverse group of disorders that impact the peripheral nerves. These conditions are characterized by either demyelination or axonal degeneration, which can lead to a range of symptoms such as diminished or altered sensation, pain, muscle weakness, and fatigue. Over time, these symptoms may contribute to secondary disabilities, which can necessitate adjustments in psychological and social functioning. Exercise therapy, aimed at enhancing strength and endurance, is often incorporated into the treatment regimen for individuals with peripheral neuropathy, particularly during the later stages of recovery from acute neuropathy or in cases of chronic neuropathy. The primary goal of this study was to evaluate the impact of exercise therapy on functional ability in individuals with peripheral neuropathy. Secondary outcomes assessed included muscle strength, endurance, broader health and well-being measures, and any adverse effects associated with the intervention. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted in September 2009 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group register, MEDLINE (from January 1966), EMBASE (from January 1980), CINAHL (from January 1982), and LILACS (from January 1982). Additionally, bibliographies of selected randomized controlled trials were reviewed, and authors were contacted to identify any further published or unpublished data. The inclusion criteria for the study required randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving individuals with peripheral neuropathy. These trials needed to compare the effects of exercise therapy with either no exercise therapy, pharmacological treatments, or alternative non-drug interventions on functional ability (or disability) for a minimum duration of eight weeks post-randomization. Two independent authors were responsible for selecting eligible studies, assessing their methodological quality, and extracting relevant data. Ultimately, only one trial fully met the inclusion criteria. Two additional trials, which evaluated outcomes within less than eight weeks post-randomization, were also included. However, the methodological quality of all three studies was suboptimal in several areas. Due to the heterogeneity of diagnostic groups and outcome measures, the data from these studies could not be pooled for analysis. The findings from the included trials did not demonstrate any significant effect of strengthening and endurance exercise programs on functional ability in individuals with peripheral neuropathy. However, there was some evidence suggesting that strengthening exercise programs had a moderate effect on improving the strength of the tested muscles. In conclusion, the available evidence is insufficient to definitively evaluate the impact of exercise therapy on functional ability in individuals with peripheral neuropathy. Nonetheless, the results indicate that progressive resistance exercise may have a beneficial effect on muscle strength in affected muscles. Further high-quality research is needed to establish the role of exercise therapy in this patient population.
